title: Multiple files, headers, and what the linker does
objective: By the end of this lesson you can split a program across files correctly, write a header that will not break, and diagnose the two link errors everyone meets.

blocks.text: A C project is a set of source files compiled separately and then joined. Each .c file becomes an object file that knows what it provides and what it still needs; the linker matches those up. Understanding that exchange makes both multi-file design and link errors straightforward.

blocks.caption: A three-file project
lines: /* math_utils.h — the interface others may use */
int add(int a, int b);          /* declaration only */
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

blocks.caption: Building it, in two ways
lines: gcc -Wall -Wextra -o prog main.c math_utils.c        # all at once
gcc math_utils.o main.o -o prog                      # then link
# Separate compilation is what lets a large project rebuild only what changed.

blocks.caption: Symbols: provided and required
lines: # Linux ELF output (macOS Mach-O normally prefixes C symbols with _)
0000000000000000 T add          <- T = defined here, in the code section
U add          <- U = undefined: needed, but not provided here
# The linker's whole job: find a T for every U.

blocks.title: The header is a promise; the .c file keeps it
blocks.text: A declaration in a header tells every file that includes it what exists and what shape it has, so calls can be checked at compile time. The definition in one .c file is what the linker actually finds. Keeping them in step is the whole discipline of multi-file C — and it is why a mismatch shows up at link time, not compile time.
Include guards, and why they are not optional

blocks.caption: Without one, a header included twice is a redefinition
lines: #ifndef MATH_UTILS_H     /* if this name is not yet defined */
#endif                   /* the second inclusion sees the name and skips everything */
/* Or, supported by every current compiler: */

blocks.text: The two link errors, and what each means

rows: Something calls foo, nothing defines it
A source file missing from the build, or a missing -l for a library
Two object files both define foo
A definition placed in a header, or a global without static

blocks.caption: The classic 'multiple definition'
lines: /* config.h — WRONG: this DEFINES a variable in every file that includes it */
/* Right: declare in the header, define in exactly one .c file */
extern int global_count;      /* declaration: it exists somewhere */
int global_count = 0;         /* definition: exactly one, here */

blocks.title: static is how you keep a name out of the link
blocks.text: Marking a function or file-level variable static means it is not exported, so it cannot collide with a same-named symbol elsewhere and cannot be called from another file. Making everything internal static is the cheapest way to keep a module's surface deliberate — and it removes a whole class of accidental coupling.

items: Declarations of functions other files may call
Type definitions those functions need in their signatures
extern declarations for shared variables — never their definitions
Constants as const or enum rather than as bare macros where possible
Nothing that allocates storage, and nothing that another file does not need

blocks.text: Header discipline that prevents slow builds

blocks.caption: Include what you use, and no more
lines: /* If the header only needs a pointer to a struct, forward-declare it: */
struct connection;                       /* no need to include connection.h */
/* Include the full definition only in the .c file that dereferences it. */
/* Every header a header includes becomes a dependency of every file
that includes it — which is how a build ends up recompiling everything

blocks.title: Build a three-file project and break it on purpose
steps: Create math_utils.h, math_utils.c and main.c as above and build with one command
Build again with -c and separate link steps
Run: nm main.o and nm math_utils.o — find the U and T entries for add
Remove math_utils.c from the link command and read the error
Move the definition of add into the header, include it from two files, and read the new error
Fix it with extern in the header and one definition in the .c file
Mark a helper function static and confirm it disappears from nm output
blocks.expected: A working multi-file build, symbol tables that show exactly what each object provides and needs, and both link errors triggered deliberately — with the fix for each one being obvious once you can read the symbols.

cheatsheet: Each .c compiles to an object file; the linker joins them
Header = declarations (a promise); one .c file = the definition
nm shows symbols: T = defined here, U = needed from elsewhere
The linker's job is to find a T for every U
Always use an include guard or #pragma once
undefined reference = missing source file in the build, or a missing -l
multiple definition = something defined in a header, or a non-static global
extern in the header, the definition in exactly one .c file
static keeps a name out of the link entirely
Forward-declare struct types in headers instead of including their full definition

checkpoint.prompt: In nm output, what does U next to a symbol mean?

choices.D: It is a universal symbol available everywhere

checkpoint.explanation: This object file needs it but does not provide it. T means defined in this object; U means required from elsewhere. Linking succeeds when every U has a matching T.

checkpoint.prompt: You get 'multiple definition of global_count'. What is the most likely cause?

choices.A: It was defined in a header
choices.C: Two functions have the same name
choices.D: The variable name is too common

checkpoint.explanation: Every file including that header defined its own copy. Declare it in the header with extern and define it in exactly one .c file. A header is included many times; a definition must exist once.

checkpoint.prompt: What does an include guard prevent?

choices.B: The header being read by the wrong compiler
choices.C: The contents of a header being processed twice in one translation unit

checkpoint.explanation: Would redefine its types. Headers commonly include other headers, so the same file arriving twice is normal. The guard makes the second arrival a no-op.

checkpoint.prompt: Why forward-declare struct connection in a header instead of including connection.h ?

choices.A: Forward declarations are faster at runtime
choices.B: A pointer does not need the full definition, and every header a header pulls in becomes a dependency of every file that includes it
choices.C: It is required by the standard
choices.D: It hides the struct from the linker

checkpoint.explanation: Include what you use. Transitive header dependencies are how one small change ends up recompiling an entire project.
